## 1. Identification Strategy
Event-study difference-in-differences (DID) within very small neighborhoods.

- Intuition: Compare sales of houses very near to an offender’s address (treated) to sales slightly farther away in the same micro-neighborhood (control) before versus after the offender’s recorded move-in (registration) date. Staggered timing across offenders and rich fixed effects absorb neighborhood-specific price trends and seasonality.
- Why appropriate: You observe precise offender move-in dates and house locations. Within-neighborhood locations of offenders are plausibly idiosyncratic conditional on neighborhood choice. This supports a within-neighborhood DID at short spatial scales. An event study around the move-in date tests pre-trends and dynamics.

## 2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable:
  - Main binary: Treated_0_10 = 1 if the sale’s parcel centroid is within 0.10 miles (528 feet; 160.9 meters) of an offender’s registered address, and the sale occurs after that offender’s registration date. Otherwise 0.
  - Distance gradient: Also estimate effects for rings: 0–0.10 mi, 0.10–0.20 mi, 0.20–0.30 mi to trace decay with distance.
- Control group:
  - Properties in the same micro-neighborhood as the offender that are 0.10–0.30 miles from the offender (or 0.15–0.30 in a robustness “donut”).
  - Control sales can occur both before and after the offender’s arrival; the identification is the differential change for near vs. farther homes within the neighborhood.
- Treatment timing / event date:
  - Event date = offender’s registration date at the specific address (proxy for move-in). Use month-level event time to reduce day-level measurement noise.
  - Event-study window: sales within [-24, +24] months of offender arrival in the baseline; expand to 48 months in robustness.
- Multiple offenders / overlap:
  - Assign each sale to the nearest offender within 0.30 miles. Drop sales within 0.30 miles of multiple offenders in a robustness test.

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Parallel trends within neighborhoods:
  - Absent the offender’s arrival, prices of near and farther houses in the same neighborhood would have evolved similarly. Plausible because neighborhoods are small (≈0.47 sq mi) and we include neighborhood-by-month fixed effects to soak up local shocks.
- No anticipation:
  - Buyers/sellers do not systematically change behavior before the recorded move-in. Plausible if public awareness is tied to the registry update; we will test for pre-trends and implement a donut around the event date.
- As-good-as-random micro-location conditional on neighborhood choice:
  - Given a neighborhood, the precise within-neighborhood address of the offender is not chosen based on very local short-run price trends. Supported by institutional details and high compliance; we add offender fixed effects to further guard against differential selection across offenders.
- Limited spillovers to the control ring:
  - The effect on 0.10–0.30 mile homes is small relative to the 0–0.10 mile homes. We will probe this via distance gradients; any spillover would attenuate estimates toward zero.

## 4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
- Endogenous micro-location correlated with micro-trends:
  - Concern: Offenders may locate near properties already trending down (e.g., near nuisance properties).
  - Remedies: 
    - Include neighborhood-by-month fixed effects to net out local shocks.
    - Include offender fixed effects to absorb offender-specific locational price levels.
    - Rich hedonic controls (size, age, quality).
    - Event-study pre-trend tests; add very local linear time trends (e.g., census block group × year trends) in robustness.
- Anticipation/measurement error in arrival date:
  - Concern: Owners learn before the registry is updated, or registration is delayed.
  - Remedies:
    - Event study to detect pre-trends.
    - Donut around event date (drop sales within ±30 or ±60 days).
    - Coarsen to month-level event time to reduce day-level mis-timing attenuation.
- Spillovers/contaminated controls:
  - Concern: Houses 0.10–0.30 miles away may also be affected.
  - Remedies:
    - Estimate full distance gradient (0–0.10, 0.10–0.20, 0.20–0.30) to characterize attenuation.
    - Use alternative control rings (e.g., 0.15–0.30) and show robustness.
    - Interpret the innermost-ring estimate as a lower bound if spillovers exist.

## 5. R Code Outline
Note: Illustrative and executable with plausible column names. Assumes three CSVs: registry.csv, parcels.csv, sales.csv.

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(lubridate)
library(geosphere)
library(fixest)
library(stringi)

#---------------------------
# 1) Load data
#---------------------------
reg <- fread("registry.csv")      # offender_id, reg_date, lat, lon, offense_type, ...
parc <- fread("parcels.csv")      # parcel_id, lat, lon, neighborhood_id, sqft, rooms, baths, quality, year_built, ...
sales <- fread("sales.csv")       # sale_id, parcel_id, sale_date, price_defl

# Parse dates
reg[, reg_date := as_date(reg_date)]
sales[, sale_date := as_date(sale_date)]

# Keep single-family homes if a flag exists (not shown); otherwise assume all are SFRs

# Merge sales with parcel characteristics and neighborhoods
dt <- merge(sales, parc, by = "parcel_id", all.x = TRUE, all.y = FALSE)

#---------------------------
# 2) Map sales to nearest offender within 0.30 miles
#---------------------------
# Distances in meters; 0.30 miles = 482.8032 meters
sales_coords <- as.matrix(dt[, .(lon, lat)])
off_coords <- as.matrix(reg[, .(lon, lat)])

D <- distm(sales_coords, off_coords, fun = distHaversine) # rows: sales, cols: offenders
min_idx <- max.col(-D)                                     # index of nearest offender
dt[, offender_id := reg$offender_id[min_idx]]
dt[, dist_m := D[cbind(.I, min_idx)]]
dt <- dt[dist_m <= 1609.34 * 0.30]                         # within 0.30 miles (482.8032 m; using 0.30*1609.34=482.8)

# Attach offender info
dt <- merge(dt, reg[, .(offender_id, reg_date)], by = "offender_id", all.x = TRUE)

#---------------------------
# 3) Construct event time, rings, treatment
#---------------------------
# Event month (coarsened)
dt[, event_month := floor(interval(reg_date, sale_date) / months(1))]  # negative before, positive after
# Window
dt <- dt[event_month >= -48 & event_month <= 48]

# Distance rings (miles)
dt[, dist_mi := dist_m / 1609.34]
dt[, ring_0_10   := as.integer(dist_mi <= 0.10)]
dt[, ring_10_20  := as.integer(dist_mi > 0.10 & dist_mi <= 0.20)]
dt[, ring_20_30  := as.integer(dist_mi > 0.20 & dist_mi <= 0.30)]

# Post dummy (allow for potential brief registration delay by adding 0 days; robustness adds donut)
dt[, post := as.integer(sale_date >= reg_date)]

# Treated = within 0.10 miles and post
dt[, treated_0_10 := as.integer(ring_0_10 == 1 & post == 1)]

# Outcome and controls
dt[, ln_price := log(price_defl)]
dt[, age := pmax(year(sale_date) - year_built, 0)]
dt[, age2 := age^2]
# Example hedonic controls (adjust for available fields)
controls <- c("log(sqft+1)", "rooms", "baths", "quality", "age", "age2")

# Fixed effects: neighborhood x year-month and offender FE
dt[, ym := format(sale_date, "%Y-%m")]
dt[, nh_ym := interaction(neighborhood_id, ym, drop = TRUE)]

#---------------------------
# 4) Main DID: ring-by-post with within-neighborhood-month FE
#---------------------------
# Use 0–0.10 as treated, 0.10–0.30 as control; estimate semi-elasticity for treated
f_main <- as.formula(paste0(
  "ln_price ~ post:ring_0_10 + ", paste(controls, collapse = " + "),
  " | nh_ym + offender_id"
))

est_main <- feols(f_main, data = dt, cluster = ~ offender_id)
etable(est_main)

# Coefficient on post:ring_0_10 is the DID estimate for <=0.10mi vs 0.10–0.30mi

#---------------------------
# 5) Event-study dynamics for 0–0.10 mi ring
#---------------------------
# Interact event_month with ring_0_10; reference month -1
est_event <- feols(
  ln_price ~ i(event_month, ring_0_10, ref = -1) + 
    log(sqft+1) + rooms + baths + quality + age + age2 | nh_ym + offender_id,
  data = dt, cluster = ~ offender_id
)
etable(est_event)

# Plot coefficients (optional)
# coefplot(est_event, simplify = TRUE)

#---------------------------
# 6) Robustness: (a) Donut around event date; (b) Alternative control ring 0.15–0.30
#---------------------------
# (a) Donut: drop sales within ±60 days of reg_date
dt[, days_to_event := as.numeric(sale_date - reg_date)]
dt_donut <- dt[abs(days_to_event) > 60]

est_donut <- feols(f_main, data = dt_donut, cluster = ~ offender_id)
etable(est_donut)

# (b) Alternative control: redefine treated and control rings
dt[, ring_0_15  := as.integer(dist_mi <= 0.15)]
dt[, ring_15_30 := as.integer(dist_mi > 0.15 & dist_mi <= 0.30)]

f_alt <- as.formula(paste0(
  "ln_price ~ post:ring_0_15 + ", paste(controls, collapse = " + "),
  " | nh_ym + offender_id"
))

est_alt <- feols(f_alt, data = dt, cluster = ~ offender_id)
etable(est_alt)

#---------------------------
# 7) Optional robustness: Repeat-sales with parcel FE
#---------------------------
# Keep parcels with at least 2 sales
rep <- dt[, .N, by = parcel_id][N >= 2]
dt_rep <- dt[parcel_id %in% rep$parcel_id]

est_repeat <- feols(
  ln_price ~ post:ring_0_10 + log(sqft+1) + rooms + baths + quality + age + age2 |
    parcel_id + ym,
  data = dt_rep, cluster = ~ offender_id
)
etable(est_repeat)
```

Notes:
- The main DID uses neighborhood-by-month FE and offender FE; the event study provides pre-trend diagnostics.
- Cluster SEs at the offender level, as treatment varies at offender-time and affects many nearby sales.
- You can add block-group × linear year trends in robustness if available.

## 6. Expected Results
- Direction: Negative. Nearby homes should sell for less after a sex offender moves in.
- Magnitude: I expect a discrete drop within 0.10 miles on the order of 2–5 percent, decaying with distance and approaching zero by 0.3 miles. Effects likely concentrated in the first months after move-in/registry update and persistent thereafter.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID/Event Study)
- C1: Parallel trends for near vs. farther homes within neighborhoods in pre-period (tested via event study) — 1
- C2: No anticipation prior to registry date — 0
- C3: No spillovers to control ring — 0
- C4: Treatment timing and micro-location as-good-as-random conditional on neighborhood and fixed effects — 1
- C5: Correct specification and inference (rich FE, hedonic controls, clustering) — 1

Overall, the design is strong if pre-trends are flat and spillovers are limited; the distance gradient and robustness checks will make the interpretation credible and transparent.
